newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German couple becomes "menage a trois".
newsitem.headline: Franco-German couple becomes "menage a trois".

text.p: The Franco-German couple, long the central relationship in European integration, became a complex "menage a trois" on Friday with France's new left-wing government adding an awkward third side to the triangle.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl put a brave face on having to deal with a French executive divided between conservative President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, holding separate meetings with each.

The three men eventually appeared side-by-side-by-side on stage at a high-tech theme park in this western French city for the final news conference and Jospin observed that "Franco-German relations transcend political alternation".
But the Paris-Bonn axis was not quite strong enough on Friday to cope with the dual challenge of a politically enfeebled German government and a divided French executive.

The two sides were not able to agree on new French demands for a European Union commitment to promote growth and jobs as well as limiting budget deficits when it launches a single European currency in 1999.
Since the upset victory of the rainbow coalition of Socialists, Communists and ecologist Greens on June 1, France has entered its third period of so-called "cohabitation" in 11 years.
"I have the advantage, or perhaps the drawback, by now of having become a specialist in cohabitation," Kohl chuckled, pronouncing the term in heavily-accented French.
The veteran chancellor recalled two previous periods of French power-sharing between the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand and conservative prime ministers.

But he might just as easily have been referring to his own uncomfortable political situation in Bonn, managing a fractious centre-right coalition and an upper house of parliament controlled by the opposition Social Democrats.
A sour aside overheard by photographers when Chirac greeted him suggested Kohl had enough headaches back home without the French left's demands for new European moves on growth and jobs.

"In Germany, we have a sort of permanent cohabitation," said an aide to Free Democratic Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, whose party has been locked in a long battle with Kohl's Christian Democrats to demand tax and public spending cuts.

As if that were not enough, the chancellor also has to cope with Finance Minister Theo Waigel's hardline Bavarian Christian Social Union, which wants the strictest possible enforcement of the criteria for a single European currency.

On the French side, Chirac played the loyal supporter of his government by urging Kohl to show understanding for the new political situation in France and accept closer coordination of European economic policies to support job-creation.

The president, who shot himself in the foot by calling a parliamentary election which his centre-right coalition lost, said the French campaign had shown that Europe had to do more to overcome a technocratic, monetarist image.
But in an apparent swipe at the left, Chirac was quoted as having told Kohl that "expectations raised during the campaign could be an additional complicating factor in meeting the criteria".

Jospin hammered home the point that if he was the unexpected star of the 69th Franco-German summit, that was largely because French voters were fed up with the unemployment and austerity they associated with European integration.

Marking his differences with Kohl on economic policy, the silver-haired premier pointedly referred to a 1994 EU agreement in Essen to launch labour-intensive public works programmes which never got off the ground because Germany has steadfastly refused to allow the EU to borrow money to fund them.
Kohl, looking stern, ruled out any extra funds or new powers for the European Commission and joked that he was "physically incapable" of being a Socialist.
